The board should treat nuclear fuel risk as a manageable procurement problem for a conventional large reactor, but as a potentially material technology and supply-chain risk for a future advanced reactor requiring HALEU. The key distinction is between uranium concentrate, which is mined and milled, and the conversion, enrichment, and fabrication services that turn it into reactor fuel. Mining is geographically concentrated: Kazakhstan supplies more than 40% of global uranium, followed by Canada, Australia, and Namibia, while Russia produces roughly 5%. Kazakhstan therefore matters, but its exposure is not simply “Russia controls the uranium”; much Kazakh material has historically travelled through Russia, and Russian interests have controlled a substantial share of Kazakh mines. The more acute concentration is downstream, because only a limited number of facilities convert uranium into uranium hexafluoride and Russia has historically supplied about one-third of global conversion output and roughly 43% of enrichment capacity. That means a utility can diversify its mining contracts yet remain exposed to a Russian-linked conversion or enrichment route, transport chokepoint, sanctions regime, or loss of qualified capacity. For an existing light-water reactor, a short disruption is less likely to cause an immediate electricity shortage because the fuel chain takes several years and utilities commonly hold inventories of three years or more. The resilience is real but not unlimited, since a prolonged disruption at conversion, enrichment, or fabrication can eventually matter even when uranium concentrate is available. Mining price headlines can therefore mislead the board: the uranium component is only about one-third of the cost of fuel loaded into a reactor, with enrichment and fabrication accounting for most of the remainder. Uranium prices can nevertheless be volatile because mine development is slow, secondary inventories can mask underlying scarcity for years, and a change from surplus to deficit can produce a sharp market response; one historical episode saw the spot price increase thirteenfold between early 2003 and mid-2007. A long-term uranium contract reduces exposure to spot-price spikes and gives a producer confidence that material is committed to a utility, but it does not by itself guarantee conversion, enrichment, fabrication slots, transport, or delivery if the contract is dependent on a politically exposed supplier. The purchase agreement should therefore require a complete, auditable fuel plan rather than merely a fixed uranium price, including named mines, conversion plants, enrichment providers, fabricators, transport routes, delivery dates, inventory ownership, substitute suppliers, and remedies for non-delivery. The utility should also separate commodity-price protection from physical-delivery protection by combining long-term contracts, diversified suppliers, minimum on-site or utility-controlled inventories, and rights to substitute non-Russian services or material. The contract should specify whether the seller is responsible for obtaining every stage of the fuel cycle or only uranium concentrate, because a concentrate contract does not solve a conversion, enrichment, fabrication, or transport bottleneck. For a conventional reactor, the board should stress-test the procurement plan against loss of Russian enrichment, loss of Russian transit, a Kazakh production interruption, a multi-year mine delay, and a sustained price increase rather than treating all risks as one generic “uranium crisis.” HALEU creates a different risk category because high-assay low-enriched uranium is enriched to about 20% uranium-235 and is required by many advanced-reactor designs, whereas conventional light-water reactors generally use a different fuel specification. The cited supply evidence identifies limited government stockpile down-blending and Russian TENEX as the available HALEU sources at that time, while domestic commercial production was absent or still being established. A future SMR decision should therefore be conditional on the vendor demonstrating an operating HALEU supply chain, qualified fuel fabricator, committed initial core inventory, reload schedule, non-Russian backup, and protection against fuel-delivery delay. The practical decision rule is that uranium supply risk alone need not be a deal-breaker for a conventional nuclear PPA, but the board should reject any proposal that presents fuel as a single commodity purchase or makes an advanced-reactor commitment before its enrichment and fuel-fabrication route is commercially secured.

The board should treat nuclear fuel risk as a manageable procurement problem for a conventional large reactor, but as a potentially material technology and supply-chain risk for a future advanced reactor requiring HALEU. [shard_01427_71709] [shard_00429_59359]

The key distinction is between uranium concentrate, which is mined and milled, and the conversion, enrichment, and fabrication services that turn it into reactor fuel. [shard_00694_6587]

Mining is geographically concentrated: Kazakhstan supplies more than 40% of global uranium, followed by Canada, Australia, and Namibia, while Russia produces roughly 5%. [shard_01427_71709]

Kazakhstan therefore matters, but its exposure is not simply “Russia controls the uranium”; much Kazakh material has historically travelled through Russia, and Russian interests have controlled a substantial share of Kazakh mines. [shard_01427_71709] [shard_04716_33903]

The more acute concentration is downstream, because only a limited number of facilities convert uranium into uranium hexafluoride and Russia has historically supplied about one-third of global conversion output and roughly 43% of enrichment capacity. [shard_01427_71709]

That means a utility can diversify its mining contracts yet remain exposed to a Russian-linked conversion or enrichment route, transport chokepoint, sanctions regime, or loss of qualified capacity. [shard_01427_71709] [shard_03242_80346]

For an existing light-water reactor, a short disruption is less likely to cause an immediate electricity shortage because the fuel chain takes several years and utilities commonly hold inventories of three years or more. [shard_00694_6587]

The resilience is real but not unlimited, since a prolonged disruption at conversion, enrichment, or fabrication can eventually matter even when uranium concentrate is available. [shard_00694_6587]

Mining price headlines can therefore mislead the board: the uranium component is only about one-third of the cost of fuel loaded into a reactor, with enrichment and fabrication accounting for most of the remainder. [shard_00407_44530]

Uranium prices can nevertheless be volatile because mine development is slow, secondary inventories can mask underlying scarcity for years, and a change from surplus to deficit can produce a sharp market response; one historical episode saw the spot price increase thirteenfold between early 2003 and mid-2007. [shard_05480_7160]

A long-term uranium contract reduces exposure to spot-price spikes and gives a producer confidence that material is committed to a utility, but it does not by itself guarantee conversion, enrichment, fabrication slots, transport, or delivery if the contract is dependent on a politically exposed supplier. [shard_03242_80346] [shard_06486_74876]

The purchase agreement should therefore require a complete, auditable fuel plan rather than merely a fixed uranium price, including named mines, conversion plants, enrichment providers, fabricators, transport routes, delivery dates, inventory ownership, substitute suppliers, and remedies for non-delivery. [shard_01427_71709] [shard_00694_6587]

The utility should also separate commodity-price protection from physical-delivery protection by combining long-term contracts, diversified suppliers, minimum on-site or utility-controlled inventories, and rights to substitute non-Russian services or material. [shard_03242_80346] [shard_00694_6587]

The contract should specify whether the seller is responsible for obtaining every stage of the fuel cycle or only uranium concentrate, because a concentrate contract does not solve a conversion, enrichment, fabrication, or transport bottleneck. [shard_00694_6587] [shard_01427_71709]

For a conventional reactor, the board should stress-test the procurement plan against loss of Russian enrichment, loss of Russian transit, a Kazakh production interruption, a multi-year mine delay, and a sustained price increase rather than treating all risks as one generic “uranium crisis.” [shard_01427_71709] [shard_00694_6587]

HALEU creates a different risk category because high-assay low-enriched uranium is enriched to about 20% uranium-235 and is required by many advanced-reactor designs, whereas conventional light-water reactors generally use a different fuel specification. [shard_05969_20472] [shard_00429_59359]

The cited supply evidence identifies limited government stockpile down-blending and Russian TENEX as the available HALEU sources at that time, while domestic commercial production was absent or still being established. [shard_05969_20472] [shard_03697_27003] [shard_05702_68807]

A future SMR decision should therefore be conditional on the vendor demonstrating an operating HALEU supply chain, qualified fuel fabricator, committed initial core inventory, reload schedule, non-Russian backup, and protection against fuel-delivery delay. [shard_00429_59359] [shard_05702_68807]

The practical decision rule is that uranium supply risk alone need not be a deal-breaker for a conventional nuclear PPA, but the board should reject any proposal that presents fuel as a single commodity purchase or makes an advanced-reactor commitment before its enrichment and fuel-fabrication route is commercially secured.
